verdict.reasoning: Patient reports wheeze starting about two days ago after dusty house cleaning: "it started, like, about two days ago" and "I was, like, cleaning the house. And, like, um, all this dust came out" and also reports shortness of breath: "I'm feeling like a little bit, uh, uh, short of breath."

Patient states the wheeze is worse at night: "Yeah. So, it get's a bit worse, um, at night, I find." Shortness of breath is part of the same symptom complex, so nocturnal worsening of breathing symptoms is directly implied.
Patient describes difficulty completing sentences when talking: "when I'm, you know, talking, um, to my friends, I start finding that, uh, sometimes, um, I'm unable to , complete my sentences."
Doctor asks about pain with deep breath and dizziness; patient denies both: "Mmm, no, no. No pain." and "Uh, no. No dizziness. Uh, none of that." Chest/pleuritic pain and dizziness are thus denied.
On oral intake: Doctor asks about eating/drinking and patient replies: "Yeah, yeah. I think I'm having, like, you know, four or five glasses a day. Yeah."
Patient states: "I used to have, like, a bit of, um, asthma, uh, as a child. Um, and, also in the summer I sometimes get, um, hay fever." This supports childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever.

Patient has an inhaler but is not taking meds for current wheeze: "I have, uh, I have, like, an asthma inhaler. I use that." and later "I think I might have one from, like, a couple of months ago." and earlier, when asked if has taken anything for the wheeze: "Uh, no. No, I haven't actually."
Patient explicitly reports prior steroid use for asthma: "I have, before, taken steroids for asthma."

Doctor asks about allergies: "apart from this, do you know if you're allergic to anything?" Patient answers: "Uh, not that I know of." This addresses general allergies, not drug allergies specifically; NKDA (no known drug allergies) is not explicitly stated.

Doctor links symptoms to asthma/allergy: "given you've got a history of asthma and hay fever. This could be one of two things. But, we want to rule out asthma or an allergy first." Symptoms described include wheeze and shortness of breath with dust exposure and nocturnal worsening, which matches the summary.

Doctor notes hay fever (allergic rhinitis) as relevant: "given you've got a history of asthma and hay fever. This could be one of two things. But, we want to rule out asthma or an allergy first." This supports a possible concurrent allergic trigger related to her allergy history.

Doctor instructs in-person GP/clinic visit with pulse oximetry: "what you'll need is visit one of our clinics, so we can do some more tests" and "use a small device on your finger, to check the amount of oxygen in your blood." The context implies current/today evaluation.

Doctor advises antihistamine trial and obtaining if not at home: "if you've got something, like an antihistamine, which you normally take for hay fever at home, I would take one" and when patient says she has none: "You might be able to get one on your way to the doctor's surgery. If not, they can prescribe you one."
Doctor states possible need for steroids depending on assessment: "you may need to take some steroids now. But, we cannot... know until we've done those tests first."

Doctor will send a letter via the app: "I'm gonna write a letter for your GP, just to let him know what's happened" and "you should get the letter over the app. And then, we can, you can take yourself to the GP."
Doctor asks distance to surgery and patient replies: "Uh, they may be minutes' drive away." indicating access within a few minutes' drive.
